Junya Watanabe
Junya Watanabe | |
|---|---|
| Born | わたなべ じゅんや 渡辺淳弥 1961 (age 64–65)[1] Fukushima, Japan |
| Alma mater | Bunka Fashion College |
| Occupation | Fashion designer |
Junya Watanabe (born 1961) is a Japanese fashion designer. He was mentored by Comme des Garçons designer Rei Kawakubo. He continues to work for Comme des Garçons; his atelier is located on the second floor of its Tokyo headquarters, and he produces four shows a year in Paris.
Biography
[edit]Born in Fukushima, Japan in 1961, Watanabe attended Bunka Fashion College in Tokyo, graduating in 1984. Soon after, he began his apprenticeship at Comme des Garçons as a patternmaker.[2][3]
In 1987, he was promoted to chief designer of Tricot knitwear line and then moved on to design for the Comme Des Garçons Homme line.
Starting in 1992, he has worked under his own name as part of Comme des Garçons, debuting his first at the concourse of Tokyo's Ryogoku Station the same year. He started his own line under the Comme Des Garçons name "Junya Watanabe Comme Des Garçons" in 1993 and began showing his womenswear in Paris that same year.[2] He debuted a men's line in 2000.[3] During the 2000-2001 Fall/Winter season, he introduced a new collection, called "Techno-culture".[4]
In 2007, Watanabe was licensed by Converse to design a series of All-Star shoes.[5] Other collaborations include Levi's, Hervier Productions, Seil Marschall, Carhartt, Nike, Merz b. Schwanen, The North Face, and ArkAir. In 2012, Watanabe designed the remote-control toy car The Hornet for the Tamiya Corporation, and released a matching pair of Reebok Pump shoes (Pump Furys).[6][7]
In March 2016, Watanabe created a solar-powered jacket/coat for his FW16 menswear line.[8] In 2020, he launched a capsule collection with Brooks Brothers.[9] He also worked with Comme des Garçons and the video game designer Yoko Taro to develop a cosplay collection.[10]
He currently continues to work for Comme des Garcons. His atelier is located on the second floor of the Comme des Garçons headquarters in Aoyama, Tokyo.[2]
Works
[edit]Watanabe often uses the word monozukuri to describe his work.[2] Watanabe is interested in synthetic and technologically advanced textiles and fabrics, but also uses more traditional materials such as cotton. He has cited Pierre Cardin and Issey Miyake as influences.[2]
Watanabe has been described as a "techno couture" designer, creating structured clothes out of modern materials.[2] His 2015 show in Paris was criticized for his use of cultural appropriation.[11] His work is considered more practical than his mentor, Rei Kawakubo's.[2]
He works with a team of 30 people and an English translator.[2] Chitose Abe formerly worked for him as a pattern-maker.[12]
Personal life
[edit]He keeps a very low profile, not appearing for the customary bow at the end of his runway shows, which he presents four times a year in Paris. He rarely gives interviews to the press, and is reticent to talk about himself in general.[2]
In popular culture
[edit]Watanabe is heavily referenced in (and is the namesake for) a song by American rappers Kanye West and Playboi Carti, titled "Junya", from West's 2021 album Donda.[13]

The Most Iconic Junya Watanabe Collaborations We Love
Junya Watanabe stands as one of the most influential figures in contemporary fashion, celebrated for his experimental approach, technical mastery, and deep respect for tradition. For more than three decades, Watanabe has challenged conventional ideas of garment construction while maintaining a strong connection to history, craftsmanship, and functionality. His work represents a careful balance between innovation and heritage, making his designs both intellectually engaging and highly wearable.
Early Life and Education
Born in Japan, Junya Watanabe graduated from the prestigious Bunka Fashion College in 1984, an institution known for producing some of the most forward thinking designers in the industry. Immediately after completing his studies, he joined Comme des Garçons as a pattern cutter. Working closely under the mentorship of Rei Kawakubo, the founder of Comme des Garçons, Watanabe developed a deep understanding of pattern-making, structure, and conceptual design. This early exposure to Kawakubo’s unconventional methods played a significant role in shaping his future aesthetic.
Rise Within Comme des Garçons
Watanabe’s talent quickly became apparent within the company. He rose through the ranks and was eventually appointed creative director of the Tricot Comme des Garçons line, a position he held until 1992. In 1993, he launched his own label, Junya Watanabe Comme des Garçons, and began presenting collections in Paris. While his early work focused primarily on womenswear, he officially introduced menswear collections in 2001, marking a major milestone in his career.
Design Philosophy and Creative Vision
What distinguishes Junya Watanabe from many of his contemporaries is his ability to reinterpret classic garments through advanced techniques and unexpected materials. His design philosophy emphasizes taking familiar wardrobe staples and transforming them into something entirely new. This mindset is famously summarized in the label found inside Junya Watanabe MAN garments, which references authenticity, history, originality, and a renewed approach to basics. Rather than chasing trends, Watanabe consistently revisits timeless silhouettes, refining and reinventing them season after season.
Innovation and Technical Experimentation
Watanabe is particularly known for his technical experimentation. Throughout his career, he has explored innovative fabrics, complex patchwork, engineered textiles, and unconventional garment construction. Despite the experimental nature of his work, functionality remains central to his designs. Jackets, coats, and trousers are not only visually striking but also practical, durable, and thoughtfully constructed. This commitment to usability has helped his menswear resonate strongly with both fashion enthusiasts and everyday wearers.
Approach to Collaborations
Another defining aspect of Junya Watanabe’s career is his pioneering approach to collaboration. Long before collaborations became a standard marketing tool in fashion, Watanabe was partnering with brands that possessed deep expertise in their respective fields. His collaborations are driven by authenticity rather than novelty, often involving manufacturers known for heritage craftsmanship and technical excellence. By working directly with specialists, Watanabe ensures that each collaborative piece remains true to its origins while reflecting his own creative vision.
Notable Collaborations
Our Favorite Junya Watanabe Collaborations
For more than 20 years, Junya Watanabe has consistently produced garments that merit long-term appreciation. Renowned for his experimental use of fabrics and advanced production methods, Watanabe has earned a reputation as one of Japan’s most influential designers. The foundation of his label lies in reworking classic wardrobe essentials with inventive ideas and unexpected details. This philosophy is clearly reflected in the label found inside every Junya Watanabe MAN garment, which reads:
Something real
Something with history and a traditional form
Our approach to originality
A renewed sense of basics
Junya Watanabe began his journey in fashion immediately after graduating from the highly respected Bunka Fashion College in 1984. Shortly after, he joined Comme des Garçons as a pattern cutter, working closely under Rei Kawakubo’s guidance. His talent and vision quickly set him apart, leading to his appointment as creative director of the Tricot knitwear line. He held this role until 1992, and in 1993 he launched his own label, “Junya Watanabe Comme des Garçons,” debuting his collections in Paris the same year. Menswear would later follow in 2001.
From the outset, Watanabe distinguished himself through an unconventional design approach. His exploration of modern textiles, experimental tailoring, and intricate pattern construction helped him build a devoted following among fashion insiders. While heavily influenced by Rei Kawakubo’s avant-garde and deconstructive techniques, Junya’s menswear has always maintained a strong connection to heritage garments and traditional craftsmanship. This balance between innovation and authenticity explains why his collaborations across various industries have been so impactful.
Watanabe places great importance on authenticity in garment development, often partnering directly with specialists with deep expertise. Although collaborations are now common throughout the fashion industry, Junya Watanabe was among the early designers to truly master the concept. While the list below is not comprehensive, it highlights some of the most memorable men’s collaborations from his career.
Junya Watanabe x Levi’s Poem Denim (2001)
Among the most coveted items in Junya Watanabe’s menswear history are the iconic Poem Jeans, first released in 2001. Crafted in collaboration with Levi’s, the denim specialists, these jeans quickly became legendary. Built upon a classic medium-wash, straight leg Levi’s silhouette, the design features screen-printed text running down the back of the left leg.
The printed poem is a collection of romantic, almost overly sentimental lines that contrast sharply with the rugged nature of denim:
Your smile makes me happy
Your voice is a bird whispering.
Your hands keep me warm.
Your perfume charms me.
Your lips are soft
You fulfill me
This early collaboration with Levi’s demonstrated the creative potential of the partnership. In later seasons, the duo expanded their work to include complex patchwork designs and digital printing techniques. The poetic text concept also resurfaced on other garments, such as shirts and outerwear, in subsequent collections.
Junya Watanabe x Porter (2004)
In 2004, Junya Watanabe joined forces with Porter to create one of the most inventive outerwear pieces of the decade. Released as part of the Spring/Summer collection, the standout item was a technical Gore-Tex rain jacket covered in an array of functional front pockets. These pockets echoed Porter’s expertise in bags and accessories, transforming the jacket into a wearable storage system.
Adding to its versatility, the jacket included a large kangaroo pocket on the back and featured a signature Porter label stitched on the front. The design went even further, allowing the jacket to be folded and converted into a tote bag by attaching straps to built-in metal loops. Although Junya Watanabe collaborated with Porter on multiple occasions, none matched the bold execution of this 2004 piece, making it a prized item among collectors and techwear enthusiasts alike.
Junya Watanabe x Vanson Leathers (2007)
Junya Watanabe’s Fall/Winter 2007 collection stands as one of his most visually striking presentations. Inspired entirely by biker culture, the collection reimagined the leather motorcycle jacket in countless forms. Elements such as collars, belts, and zippers were dismantled and redistributed across various garments, while runway models reinforced the theme by wearing full motorcycle helmets.
To execute the leather pieces authentically, Watanabe collaborated with Vanson Leathers, a renowned American manufacturer of motorcycle apparel. The resulting jackets closely followed traditional rider silhouettes, enhanced by subtle design touches such as camouflaged interior linings. Notably, the garments retained full functionality, using heavyweight competition-grade calf leather suitable for actual riding. In later seasons, Junya continued his partnership with Vanson, expanding into varsity jackets, leather bags, and other classic American-inspired pieces.
Junya Watanabe x Brooks Brothers (2009)
Brooks Brothers, the oldest men’s clothier in the United States, is synonymous with classic American tailoring. Junya Watanabe began collaborating with the heritage brand in 2009, focusing primarily on two of its most iconic garments: the button down Oxford shirt and the blazer.
Watanabe reinterpreted the Oxford shirt with a softer, more relaxed silhouette, rounded hems, and a slimmer fit, while preserving the traditional collar. He introduced contrasting fabrics such as gingham and plaid, adding visual interest to the otherwise classic designs. The blazers followed a similar philosophy, incorporating patchwork elements and, in some cases, reversible construction, offering fresh perspectives on timeless staples.
Junya Watanabe x Hervier Productions (2012)
For Fall/Winter 2012, Junya Watanabe drew inspiration from traditional workwear and collaborated with French brand Hervier Productions. The collection centered on jackets and trousers made from durable materials, including cotton twill, moleskin, and wool blends.
Classic workwear features, including metal rivets and functional pocket layouts, were combined with refined details such as paisley-lined interiors. The collaboration spanned multiple seasons and was notable for being priced more accessibly than many of Watanabe’s usual offerings, broadening its appeal without sacrificing craftsmanship.
Junya Watanabe x Loewe (2014)
In 2014, Junya Watanabe partnered with Spanish luxury house Loewe to celebrate the brand’s 40th anniversary in Japan. Known for its mastery of leather, Loewe proved an ideal collaborator. Watanabe described the concept as a fusion of both brands’ identities, blending Loewe’s luxurious leatherwork with Junya’s denim expertise.
The collection leaned heavily into punk influences, featuring zippers, tartan patterns, and patchwork throughout. Leather garments stood out for their ability to balance rebellious styling with refined luxury, while travel bags emerged as particularly memorable highlights of the collaboration.
Junya Watanabe x The North Face (2017)
Junya Watanabe’s Fall/Winter 2017 show in Paris unveiled his collaboration with outdoor brand The North Face. Inspired by 1990s hip hop culture, the collection placed strong emphasis on equipment and functionality, particularly drawing from The North Face’s iconic duffel bags.
High-quality materials sourced from Japan were used to deconstruct and reconstruct these bags into wearable garments. One standout piece was a varsity jacket made from PVC fabric from duffel bags, complete with oversized branding on the back. Additional items included work jackets and nylon parkas, seamlessly blending Junya’s design language with The North Face’s outdoor heritage. The collection stands as a powerful example of how past influences can be reimagined into modern collector-worthy pieces.
Redefining Heritage Brands
Watanabe’s partnership with Brooks Brothers showcased his ability to reimagine traditional American tailoring. By subtly altering proportions, introducing patchwork, and experimenting with reversibility, he brought new life to classic shirts and blazers. His work with Hervier Productions drew inspiration from French workwear, emphasizing durability and honest construction while incorporating refined details. The collaboration with Loewe merged luxury leather craftsmanship with punk-inspired styling, while his partnership with The North Face redefined outdoor gear through deconstruction and streetwear influences.
Japanese Craftsmanship and Global Influence
Despite his global recognition, Junya Watanabe remains deeply rooted in Japanese design values. Precision, discipline, and respect for materials are evident in every collection. His garments often require advanced manufacturing processes, reflecting a level of craftsmanship that aligns closely with traditional Japanese production standards. This dedication to quality has earned him a loyal following among collectors and fashion insiders who value substance over hype.
Legacy and Impact on Modern Fashion
In the modern fashion landscape, where trends change rapidly and mass production dominates, Junya Watanabe’s work stands apart. He continues to push boundaries without losing sight of functionality or heritage. His designs challenge the wearer to think differently about clothing, encouraging appreciation for construction, material, and purpose. Whether through standalone collections or carefully considered collaborations, Watanabe consistently demonstrates that innovation and tradition can coexist.
Conclusion
Today, Junya Watanabe’s influence extends far beyond the runway. His work has shaped the direction of contemporary menswear, inspiring designers to explore new possibilities while respecting the past. As fashion continues to evolve, Junya Watanabe remains a vital force, proving that true originality comes not from abandoning history but from reinterpreting it with intelligence and creativity.

Doraemon Streetwear, Clothing, Hoodie, and History: The Complete Cultural & Fashion Guide
Few characters in the international pop culture lexicon have managed to attain the same level of timeless appeal and multi-generational impact as Doraemon. What began as a simple manga series in Japan has since grown into a worldwide cultural phenomenon that encompasses everything from animation and film to toys, digital media, and, more recently, streetwear and fashion collections. Today, Doraemon is more than simply a retro cartoon character; it is a brand, a symbol, and a lifestyle influence that bridges the gap between childhood nostalgia and modern design culture.
Doraemon streetwear, clothing, and hoodie collections have become an integral part of the modern fashion scene. This article examines the history and future potential of Doraemon, its brand identity, merchandise empire, and collaborations, with a particular emphasis on its growing impact within the streetwear culture.
The History and Background of Doraemon
Doraemon was born in 1969 from the minds of the famous Japanese manga artist Fujiko Fujio and was first published by Shogakukan in children’s magazines. Essentially, the plot revolves around a robotic cat from the future named Doraemon, who travels back in time from the 22nd century to help a young boy named Nobita Nobi, whose poor choices jeopardize the future of his family. Doraemon has been sent back in time by Nobita’s descendant with the sole purpose of helping him lead a better life through the use of his four-dimensional pocket full of high-tech gadgets.
What makes Doraemon the phenomenon that it is, is its incredibly simple yet profoundly rich storyline: a poor, unfortunate child is provided with access to high-tech gadgets that can solve all his problems instantly—but often with unforeseen results. By using this framework, the series masterfully weaves together science fiction, comedy, and real-life situations with moral teachings. Each and every one of these stories explores concepts such as responsibility, hard work, and the value of personal development, all of which convey the message that success in life cannot be achieved through shortcuts alone.
Why Doraemon Became Timeless
The secret to the success of Doraemon is that it has been able to convey universal human values in a simple yet effective manner. Essentially, the series delves into issues such as friendship, taking responsibility, the effects of shortcutting, and learning from one’s mistakes. Every episode is a reflection of real-life issues, whether it is coping with failure, peer pressure, or self-doubt, making the series extremely relevant to both children and adults. While children are able to relate to the comedic elements and the gadgets, adults are able to relate to the emotional aspects. This has made Doraemon extremely relevant across generations, and it has been able to maintain its position in the market for several decades. The manga series has sold more than 170 million copies, making it one of the best-selling manga series of all time.
From Stage to Screen to Streetwear
Doraemon’s journey from manga to global fashion influence is a unique evolution.
Anime Expansion
Doraemon’s growth accelerated significantly through its television adaptations, which played a crucial role in transforming it from a manga series into a global phenomenon. The first anime adaptation aired in 1973, but it was a short-lived production that remained obscure. However, the 1979–2005 series became iconic, running for decades and establishing Doraemon’s classic visual identity and storytelling style. The 2005 reboot modernized animation and expanded international reach, helping Doraemon gain popularity across Asia, Europe, and other global markets.
Film Industry Growth
The Doraemon film series, which began in 1980, significantly expanded the franchise’s narrative depth and global appeal by introducing longer, more cinematic storytelling. Unlike episodic television formats, these films explore grand adventures, emotional character development, and complex themes such as friendship, sacrifice, and personal growth. Notable titles like Stand by Me Doraemon utilized modern CGI animation and heartfelt storytelling, attracting both nostalgic longtime fans and a new generation of viewers, further strengthening Doraemon’s cultural impact.
Transition into Fashion
As nostalgia-driven fashion trends started gaining traction worldwide, Doraemon was able to seamlessly transition into the streetwear and lifestyle fashion trend, evolving from a nostalgic childhood character to a modern-day icon. The brand collaborated with renowned designers and brands to launch graphic tees with iconic prints, limited edition Doraemon hoodies, exclusive designer collaborations, and curated capsule collections. These fashion items not only symbolize nostalgia but also cater to the adult market looking for fun and creative outlets. By combining childhood nostalgia with modern design, Doraemon has emerged as a distinctive link between intergenerational fan loyalty and fashion-forward streetwear.
The Brand Identity
Doraemon’s brand identity is a mix of nostalgia, innovation, playfulness, and moral storytelling, which makes it a universally appealing and timeless presence in popular culture. Nostalgia is a link between generations who have grown up reading the manga series or watching the anime series, which reminds them of their childhood. Innovation is not only seen in Doraemon’s gadgets but also in the fact that the series has been adapting to modern media, fashion, and technology. Playfulness is seen in Doraemon’s design, humor, and adventures, which makes it accessible and interesting, and moral storytelling teaches them the lessons of responsibility, friendship, perseverance, and creativity.
Visual Identity
The visual identity of Doraemon is easily recognizable because of the unique blend of design elements that have a wide appeal to all age groups. The iconic blue robotic cat design with a white face, round eyes, and a red collar gives the impression of being friendly and approachable. The use of rounded shapes and soft edges gives the impression of being playful and harmless, and the addition of sci-fi gadgets like the Anywhere Door or the Bamboo Copter adds to the imaginative and sci-fi aspects of the character.
Emotional Branding
One of the most appealing aspects of Doraemon is its emotional branding, which has been made possible through the strong emotional connections that the franchise has been able to establish with its audience. The franchise takes the audience back to their childhood memories of fun-filled adventures, school, and storytelling, and also focuses on the struggles that they have been able to overcome, such as school, development, and learning from mistakes. The emotional and feel-good stories of the franchise have been able to create a strong sense of nostalgia and emotional connection with the audience. This is why the products of the franchise, such as its clothing, hoodies, and collectibles, are so desirable.
Who Owns A Doraemon?
The ownership and operation of the Doraemon franchise are shared by several major organizations, such as Fujiko Pro, Shogakukan, TV Asahi, Shin Ei Animation, and ADK Emotions, each contributing in a unique way to the continued global reach of the franchise. The original authors, Fujiko F. Fujio, are operating through their production company, Fujiko Pro, which is managing the creative direction, character consistency, and approval of new content. In addition to Fujiko Pro, TV Asahi, a large Japanese broadcasting network, is managing the production and broadcasting of the anime series, ensuring that Doraemon reaches a wide television audience both in Japan and worldwide. At the same time, Shin Ei Animation, a major animation studio, is managing the technical and artistic side of animation production, ensuring that the high-quality visuals and consistent character design, which have become recognizable worldwide, are maintained.
These organizations are working together to manage several aspects of the franchise, including content production, global distribution, and licensing agreements. A special division of Shogakukan Shueisha Productions (ShoPro) is managing the entire licensing business for merchandising and promotional activities both in Japan and worldwide.This structured ownership framework ensures that Doraemon operates not just as a popular cartoon but as a strategically managed intellectual property, capable of sustaining long term growth, cultural relevance, and commercial success across multiple industries and international markets. It is this careful stewardship that has cemented Doraemon’s place as a global cultural icon.
Country of Origin
Doraemon originated from Japan, a nation that has earned international recognition for its vibrant and iconic anime and manga culture. Doraemon appeared in the late 1960s when Japan had a strong creative industry that offered a conducive environment for the development of innovative storytelling, character creation, and manga production.
The Japanese elements in Doraemon, which combined creative science fiction, moral education, and real-life experiences, appealed to many people both locally and internationally. Over the years, Doraemon has transformed from a source of entertainment to a cultural icon that represents Japanese creativity, morality, and technological imagination in international platforms. Its universal appeal has made it a global entertainment brand, which has reached many people in Asia, Europe, and the Americas through manga, anime, movies, and other merchandise.
In 2008, the Japanese government acknowledged the cultural significance of Doraemon by appointing it as an anime ambassador. This appointment recognizes the significance of the character in promoting Japanese culture internationally. Currently, Doraemon represents not only nostalgia and storytelling but also the Japanese spirit of innovation, artistic perfection, and international cultural influence.
A Doraemon Product Line
Likewise, the toy and collectible segment also comprises a large part of the product range. Ranging from action figures and plush toys to gadget replicas and limited edition collectibles, these products target not only children but also collectors, thereby bridging the gap between nostalgia and contemporary consumer culture. Collectibles also provide an avenue for community engagement, as fans engage in trading, forums, and exhibitions that showcase the rich history of the franchise.
Stationery products featuring Doraemon characters, such as notebooks, pens, stationery, and planners, further expand the reach of the franchise into the daily lives of consumers. These products not only have a functional use but also provide a lifestyle statement, as they enable fans to integrate a beloved cultural icon into their daily activities. Educational stationery also aligns with the franchise’s underlying themes of responsibility, creativity, and learning, thereby increasing its appeal to parents and educators looking for engaging tools for children.
However, the most rapidly growing category in the current product range of Doraemon is fashion, specifically clothing and streetwear lines. The growing trend of nostalgia-based fashion and the popularity of character-based apparel have created a lucrative market for Doraemon clothing. This includes graphic tees, hoodies, jackets, caps, and bags that have iconic scenes, character designs, and futuristic gadget motifs. Fashion collaborations with streetwear brands such as Gucci, Uniqlo, and others have pushed the character from being a childhood icon to a modern-day fashion icon. These collaborations have also led to limited edition lines that combine playful design with high-end streetwear fashion, creating massive hype and demand around the world. Doraemon clothing is also a hit with the older generation who grew up with the character, giving fans a chance to showcase their personal nostalgia while also staying on top of modern fashion trends.
The rise of Doraemon streetwear also shows the adaptability and relevance of the brand. By combining nostalgia, creativity, and lifestyle, Doraemon has evolved from a manga character to a diverse product ecosystem. Today, with its presence in the entertainment, gaming, collectibles, stationery, and fashion sectors, it is ensured that Doraemon remains relevant to a broad range of fans across generations and sectors, while also retaining a consistent and recognizable brand identity across the world.
Apparel & Accessories
The impact of Doraemon on the fashion industry has been immense in the last ten years, especially in the casual and street fashion industry, where nostalgic characters and designs have become a huge trend. The brand has managed to turn its iconic characters into wearable art, making fashion a huge part of its product line. Some of the most popular fashion items include Doraemon hoodies, which come with bold designs of the character or his futuristic gadgets, combining comfort and design. King Schools, Inc. is an American computer software company headquartered in San Diego, California. The company focuses on the creation of Computer Based Training (CBT) or e-learning to assist individuals in obtaining all levels of pilot certification in the United States. Over the years, the company has expanded its training courses to cover the various pilot certificates, ratings and educational requirements, along with many aeronautical elective studies. More recently, it has begun offering all of its courses in web-based training (WBT) and mobile device formats.
King Schools was founded in 1974 by John and Martha King, husband and wife. As Certified Flight Instructors, the Kings first began as a traveling ground school, offering two-day courses in various cities. A little more than a decade later, they began producing training videos that other flight instructors could incorporate into their own curriculum. Eventually, demand for their videos by individuals learning to fly led to the development of courses that could be used for self-paced study.[2]
As of May 2010, King Schools has over 70 employees and operates exclusively from an 18,000-square-foot (1,700 m2) facility near Montgomery Field (KMYF) in San Diego.[1] Course development, production, customer service and shipping all occur at this location. Course videos are filmed either in the in-house digital studio or at nearby Montgomery Field.
John and Martha King are two of the most recognized experts in flight instruction,[3][4][5] and King Schools is best known for its effective use of a folksy, humor-rich approach in their training videos. The company claims that more than half of all pilots in the United States have studied using one of their courses. Of the courses they offer, the Private Pilot Knowledge Test Course is likely the most used, supporting FAA Part 61 ground schools. Among the approximately 90 other courses offered, topics covered include Private Pilot, Instrument Pilot, Commercial Pilot, International Operations and risk management. King Schools also produces the Cessna-branded courses used by Cessna Pilot Centers, which are Part 141 ground schools.[6]
History
[edit]- In 1975, King Schools, Inc. was started by John and Martha King as a touring two-day ground school.
- In 1989, King Schools moves to its current facility in San Diego, near Montgomery Field
- In 1999, King Schools produces the flight training videos for Microsoft Flight Simulator 2000, featuring John and Martha King providing personal instruction for virtual pilots. They also did the same for Microsoft Flight Simulator 2002, in 2001.[7]
In 2008, the Kings were inducted into the International Air & Space Hall of Fame at the San Diego Air & Space Museum, and in 2019, they were inducted into the National Aviation Hall of Fame at the National Museum of the United States Air Force.[8]
Flying risk awareness advocacy
[edit]In March 2001, Flying magazine published an interview with John King titled "John King's Crusade to Change Aviation's Culture."[9] In the article, John openly charged the general-aviation industry with mischaracterizing that light aircraft could be considered safe. He argued that general aviation pilots were insufficiently trained to recognize and address flight hazards. King Schools later joined efforts with Avemco Insurance to produce a training video to do this.[10] In 2003, this led to the first in a series of training videos marketed by King Schools as a "Practical Risk Management" course.[11]

Glipodes dietrichi is a type of beetle that belongs to the Glipodes genus. It is part of the Mordellidae family, which are often called "tumbling flower beetles." This specific beetle was first described in 1962 by a scientist named Franciscolo.
Contents
What are Tumbling Flower Beetles?
Glipodes dietrichi is a member of the Mordellidae family. These beetles are known for their unique shape. They have a humpbacked body and a head that points downwards. Their bodies are usually wedge-shaped. This helps them move around easily.
Why are they called "Tumbling Flower Beetles"?
These beetles get their name from how they move. They can tumble and jump very quickly. This helps them escape from predators. They are often found on flowers. They visit flowers to feed on pollen and nectar.
Where Do They Live?
Tumbling flower beetles, including Glipodes dietrichi, are found in many parts of the world. They prefer warm and temperate climates. You can often spot them in gardens, meadows, and forests. They like places where there are plenty of flowering plants.
What Do They Eat?
Adult Glipodes dietrichi beetles mostly eat pollen and nectar. They play a role in pollination as they move from flower to flower. This helps plants reproduce. The larvae (young beetles) of Mordellidae beetles have a different diet. They usually live inside decaying wood or plant stems. They feed on the decaying plant material. Some larvae might also be predators of other small insects.
Life Cycle of a Beetle
Like all beetles, Glipodes dietrichi goes through a complete metamorphosis. This means they have four main stages in their life.
Egg Stage
The life cycle begins when the female beetle lays her eggs. She usually places them in cracks in wood or on plant stems. The eggs are tiny and often hard to see.
Larva Stage
After hatching, the eggs turn into larvae. These larvae look like small worms. They spend their time eating and growing. They shed their skin several times as they get bigger. This process is called molting.
Pupa Stage
Once the larva is fully grown, it enters the pupa stage. During this stage, the larva transforms into an adult beetle. The pupa is usually still and does not eat. It's like a resting phase where big changes happen inside.
Adult Stage
Finally, the adult beetle emerges from the pupa. The adult beetle is ready to find a mate. It will then lay its own eggs to start the cycle again. Adult beetles are the ones you see flying around and visiting flowers.
Importance of Beetles
Beetles are a very diverse group of insects. They play many important roles in nature.
- Pollinators: Many beetles, like Glipodes dietrichi, help pollinate plants.
- Decomposers: Some beetles help break down dead plants and animals. This returns nutrients to the soil.
- Food Source: Beetles are food for many other animals, such as birds and small mammals.
- Pest Control: Some beetles eat insects that are harmful to crops.

A classical-techno masterpiece! Get it if you can find it!
Reader review by Jon Turner (2008-06-04)
Upon listening to the music to Actraiser, one has the impression that it sounds and feels very symphonic. The compositions themselves sparkle with classical leitmotifs very much in the style of Bach, Beethoven, Mozart, Bruckner, or Mahler, but it's the sampled "orchestra" driving them which really makes this score tick. Squeezing out the limits of the much-heralded Super Nintendo sound chip, Yuzo Koshiro manages to create a rich, vibrant synthesis that very closely resembles, but never quite sounds identical to, an actual orchestra. For a system that relied on cartridges for its games, this was a very impressive achievement indeed.
There is really no way to describe the score for Actraiser as anything but a masterpiece. The first track of the score, a rousing, heroic march introduced by the rich tones of the brass section, immediately displays its epic nature. This is followed by "Sky Palace", a slow, melancholy hymn reminiscent of Bach's "Tocatta and Fugue in D Minor", delivered on a heavy-sounding pipe organ.
When the action stages kick into gear, so too does the score, as Koshiro meshes the classical tones with an interesting techno tempo, as evidenced in "Filmoa". This track mixes another Bach-style composition with an impressive percussion beat. It's as if Bach's Brandenburg concertos have gone disco! While the remaining tracks don't exactly match this amazing mixture, they fall no short of excellence. "Blood Pool ~ Casandora" and "All Over the World" sizzle with energy and power, while "Aitos ~ Temple" begins ominously before moving to an understated but intense tempo. Quieter breaks include the minimalistic-sounding "Pyramid ~ Marana" and the warm yet romantic "North Wall". This latter track reminds me a lot of Holst's "Venus" movement from his Planets score.
The boss battle themes, which include "The Beast Appears", "Powerful Enemy", and "Satan", are some of the most furious, fast-paced, pounding action cues ever committed to a video game. Additionally three of the eighteen tracks on the album are classified as fanfares, with "Silence" being the standout among them.
For the simulation stages, Koshiro tones down the intensity and turns up the subtleness and warmth. "Birth of the People" is a Mozart-like concerto carried by the pizzicato plucks of strings and the mellow, almost heavenly tones of woodwinds. "Offering" is a beautiful, heartfelt hymn that displays Koshiro at his finest and the Super Nintendo sound chip at its most pleasing. The penultimate track "Peaceful World" depicts a triumphant yet restrained epilogue that conveys newfound harmony.
The score's final track begins sounding something along the lines of the 20th Century Fox fanfare before settling into a victorious march. Midway through, a brief reprise of "North Wall" can be heard just prior to a grand finale that culminates with four very satisfying notes.
Tracks loop two to three times and are amplified by a rich, studio-like reverb added primarily to give the tunes a more concert-like feel. Considering that much of Actraiser's score screams "classical", this is a nice bonus. Recently, perhaps due to the game being re-released on the Wii Virtual Console, the score has been made available again on a three-disc compilation from Five Records, "Yuzo Koshiro Best Collection Vol. 1". While this album includes a four-second track omitted from the original release ("Level Up", a brief harp glissando fanfare), the sound mix in this newer release omits the concert-like feel, resulting in a less full experience.
The publishing situation aside, there is no denying that Actraiser is an amazing early example of game music at its finest. Future game scores have become more elaborate, complex, and experimental, but it's remarkable how well Actraiser holds up to them to this day. As a cartridge-based score it is phenomenal. Finicky listeners may gripe at how dated the synthesis sounds at times, but on the whole this remains a soundtrack of excellence, exuding an epic classical style seldom matched.

Self Portrait with Loose Hair, 1947 by Frida Kahlo
In 1946, Frida's health got worse and she made a trip to New York for a spinal fusion surgery. This operation was called "the beginning of the end" by Frida Kahlo since after this operation, her condition has been getting worse and worse even she consulted so many doctors and specialists. This self-portrait was painted while she was recovering from this surgery. Frida looks thin and exhausted in this painting. The legend on the scroll at the bottom of this painting reads:
Here I painted myself, Frida Kahlo, with my reflection in the mirror. I am 37 years old and this is July, 1947. In Coyoacan, Mexico, the place where I was born".
She stated herself as "37 years old" in the inscription but her real age was 40 at the time this portrait was painted.
In this painting, Frida depicted herslef with a large volume of loose hair. It probably because she wants to please Diego Rivera since he is obsessed with her long hair.
This painting was auctioned by Christie's, New York, in May of 1991. It was sold for a wowing price of $1,650,000.
In the 2003 Miramax Film "FRIDA", actress Salma Hayek played the role of Frida. Salma herself is an amateur artist and painted her own version of this portrait during the time she was shooting this film.

full_text:
Kahlo was seriously hurt in a traffic accident when she was 18 years old and her injuries plagued her for her entire life.
At a stroke the incident ended her dreams of becoming a doctor and left her with debilitating pain and disability that continually worsened as she grew older.
Unlike previous treatments the aim was to actually fuse her spine together and was a much more drastic intervention.
Having consulted numerous doctors the surgery was deemed to be her best course of action but as time passed after the operation her condition continually worsened. Kahlo describes the procedure as "the beginning of the end."
In the self-portrait Kahlo appears thin and tired but also has an air of relaxation with her mouth close to smiling. Her hair, often used by Kahlo to express her emotions in her paintings, is thick and flowing and an exaggeration of how her hair was at the time.
This may have been to please her husband, Diego Rivera, who obsessed over her long hair.
At the bottom of the painting the scrolled parchment reads: "Here I painted myself, Frida Kahlo, with my reflection in the mirror. I am 37 years old and this is July, 1947. In Coyoacan, Mexico, the place where I was born". In reality her age was 40 years old.
The painting sold at auction in May 1991 at Christie's in New York and fetched a price of $1,650,000.
The 2003 film entitled "Frida" starred Salma Hayek playing the lead role of Kahlo. Hayek was a keen amateur artist and during filming and in her spare time she painted her own version of this work.

Kahlo Self-Portrait Goes for Record $1.65 Million
- Share via
Frida Kahlo’s “Self-Portrait With Loose Hair” sold for a record $1.65 million Wednesday night at Christie’s New York. The 1947 painting is the most expensive work by a Latin American artist ever sold at auction, surpassing the previous record price of $1.43 million paid last year for another Kahlo self-portrait, “Diego y Yo.”
The Park Avenue auction house identified the buyer only as a Mexican private collector, but sources who attended the auction said that the new owner of the highly publicized Kahlo is Margara Garza-Sada of Monterrey, Mex. Her son, Mauricio Fernandez, is said to have made the winning bid. Sources familiar with Garza-Sada’s collection said that she is a major collector of Mexican art.
“Self-Portrait With Loose Hair,” which had been valued at $1.5 million to $2 million, was the highlight of a two-day auction of Latin American art scheduled to wind up late Thursday afternoon. The auction of 216 items is expected to total between $12.4 million and $16.2 million in sales.
The Kahlo painting was sold by Louise Noun of Des Moines, who has established the Chrysalis Foundation to benefit Iowa women through scholarships and innovative programs. Proceeds of the sale will endow an archive for Iowa women at the University of Iowa. Noun bought the painting for $85,000 in 1983.

OdishaResearchers validate India’s first dichromatic snake species
A century-old confusion on existence of a snake which is sexually dichromatic __ colours of male and female are different __ have been resolved by a group of biologists who have also validated it as
BHUBANESWAR: A century-old confusion on existence of a snake which is sexually dichromatic __ colours of male and female are different __ have been resolved by a group of biologists who have also validated it as a different species for the first time.
The reptile has been renamed as Variable Coloured Vine Snake, the species name being Ahaetulla anomala. This is also for the first time that sexually dichromatism among snakes has been discovered in Indian subcontinent, which is considered a significant feat.
The snake’s presence is limited to Odisha, West Bengal, Jharkhand, Bihar and Bangladesh. For more than 100 years, its separate colour scheme used to get the females clubbed with Brown Vine Snake and the males with Common Vine Snake. The females of the Variable Coloured Vine Snake are brown while the males are an attractive green.
The team of biologists, comprising Pratyush Mohapatra, Prof S K Dutta, Abhijit Das, Niladri Kar, BHCK Murthy and V Deepak conducted molecular and morphological study of the snake to separate it from the Common Vine Snakes. The snake was first spotted near North Orissa University campus in Baripada by Mohapatra and Dutta in 2007, who initiated the study to find out more about the species. “We encountered both green and brown morphs of this subspecies in the repository of ZSI, Kolkata collected from West Bengal, Jharkhand and Bihar, some of which were catalogued as Ahaetulla pulverulenta,” revealed a peer reviewed paper by the six biologists in Zootaxa, an international journal of repute on taxonomy.
The snake was first described by Thomas Nelson Annandale, the first Director General of Zoological Society of India, in 1906. “Apart from several individuals of the species, we also studied the original specimen by Annadale before delving into the molecular and morphology analysis.
We found out that the colour difference between the male and female was the major reason for which this species was confused as a different species,” said Mohapatra, who is a scientist with ZSI at its Central Zone Regional Centre at Jabalpur in Madhya Pradesh.
During the research study that lasted for a decade, the team found that Brown Vine Snake, with which this species was mixed up, is seen in Western Ghats and Sri Lanka while two scientists in 2010 had found the species in Bangladesh. This led to confusion as to how the snake was seen at all these places and the team went into deeper DNA analysis which validated that the Variable Coloured Vine Snake is a valid species and its dichromatic nature came to fore, said Prof Dutta, a pioneer herpetologist and co-author of the paper.
“Sexual dichromatism is rare among snakes and until now documented in some groups such as vipers, Comoran snake and Malagasy leaf-nosed snakes Langaha madagascariensis. Ahaetulla anomala is therefore the first reported sexually dichromatic snake from the Indian subcontinent,” the research paper said.

Its prominent, longer dermal appendage distinguishes it from other species of Ahaetulla found in India and Sri Lanka except A. nasuta and A. pulverulenta. Morphologically A. anomala differs from all forms of A.nasuta in having its dermal appendage covered by many small scales above (vs. dermal appendage formed by rostral scale only); it has a dark rhomboidal pattern on the dorsal surface of the head (vs. no dorsal head marking); in A. anomala the asulcate side of hemipenis has 3–5 nude grooves (vs. 5–7 in A. nasuta Odisha population). Though the brown colour forms (adult females) of A. anomala are superficially similar to A. pulverulenta, it differs from the latter in: length of dermal appendage shorter than horizontal eye diameter (vs. always longer in adults); sexual dichromatism- body colouration of adult males are green and females brown (vs. always brown or greyish- brown); dorsal scales at one head length before vent – 11 rows, rarely 13 in females and 9 in males (vs. mostly in 13 rows). The hemipenis of A. anomala also differs in structure from that of A. pulverulenta (Western Ghats specimens) in bearing 5–6 large spines on the asulcate side (vs. 8–9 large spines) [MOHAPATRA et al 2017] |

Sexual dichromatism. Various authors have mentioned polymorphism in ground colour in snakes such as Boiga forsteni, Sonora semiannulata and Psammophis schokari (Mohapatra et al. 2009; Cox 2012; Hussain & Hussain 2013). In a recent publication, Cox and Chippindale (2014) suggested that despite dramatic color polymorphism in Sonora semiannulata, phenotypic diversity is not a major driver of genetic diversity within or among populations. Similarly Ahaetulla anomala shows colour polymorphism and has a gradient of green and brown colours. As stated earlier, adult males of this species are green coloured and adult females are brown in colour. Among the specimens examined, the greyish-green coloured individual is a juvenile male and the greyish brown individual is a juvenile female. These intermediate colours could be an artefact of ontogenic colour change (See Deepak et al. 2010). Sexual dichromatism is rare among snakes and until now documented in some groups such as vipers (Vipera, Bothrops) (Shine & Madsen 1994; Lindell & Forsman 1996; Marques & Sazima 2003; de Freitas et al. 2014), Comoran snake (Lycodryas) (Hawlitschek et al. 2012) and Malagasy leaf-nosed snakes Langaha madagascariensis (Krysko 2003). Template:Arvind Kejriwal series Arvind Kejriwal (hi; born 16 August 1968) is an Indian politician, activist and former bureaucrat, who served as the 7th Chief Minister of Delhi. He was the chief minister from 2013 to 2014 and from 2015 to 2024. He is also the national convener of the Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) since 2012. He represented the New Delhi constituency in the Delhi Legislative Assembly from 2015 to 2025, and previously from 2013 to 2014.
In 2006, Kejriwal was awarded the Ramon Magsaysay Award for his involvement in the Parivartan movement using right to information legislation in a campaign against government corruption. The same year, after resigning from government service, he founded the Public Cause Research Foundation to campaign for transparent governance. Before entering politics, Kejriwal had worked in the Indian Revenue Service. Prior to that, he was a mechanical engineer from IIT Kharagpur.
In 2012, he launched the AAP. In 2013, he assumed office as the Chief Minister of Delhi and resigned 49 days later over his inability to mobilise support for his proposed anti-corruption legislation. In the 2015 Delhi Legislative Assembly elections, the AAP registered an unprecedented majority. In subsequent 2020 elections, AAP re-emerged victorious and retained power in Delhi, following which, Kejriwal was sworn in as the Chief Minister of Delhi for the third time in a row. Outside Delhi, his party registered another major victory in 2022 Punjab Legislative Assembly election.
He was arrested on 21 March 2024 by the Enforcement Directorate on allegations of a liquor scam against the Aam Aadmi Party led Delhi Government.[1][2] He became the first ever sitting chief minister in India to be arrested.[3] His other party leaders, Satyendra Jain, Sanjay Singh and Manish Sisodia have also spent months to years in jail without bail, trial or conviction.[4] The opposition alliance called the arrest weeks before the 2024 Indian general election, a case of fabrication and "match-fixing" by the BJP. Amnesty International said that financial and terrorism laws have been weaponised to go after political opponents.[5] On 10 May, the Supreme Court ordered Kejriwal's release on interim bail until 1 June 2024, on account of campaigning for the election.[6][7] Kejriwal surrendered at Tihar Jail after the expiry of his bail period on 2 June 2024. On 13 September 2024, he was granted bail by Supreme Court with certain conditions, the case still continues.[8] On 17 September 2024, he resigned as Delhi Chief Minister saying he will only become CM again if he receives a public mandate.[9]
His party suffered a heavy defeat in the 2025 Delhi Legislative Assembly election, with he himself losing his seat to Parvesh Verma by a margin of over 4,000 votes from the New Delhi Assembly constituency along with many other notable AAP members. On 27 February 2026, he was granted a clean chit in the excise policy case, along with 22 others, inculding Manish Sisodia.[10]
Early life and career[edit | edit source]
Kejriwal was born in a Haryanvi Agrawal-Baniya[11] family in Siwani in the Bhiwani district of Haryana, India on 16 August 1968, the first of the three children of Gobind Ram Kejriwal and Gita Devi. His father was an electrical engineer who graduated from the Birla Institute of Technology, Mesra. Kejriwal spent most of his childhood in north Indian towns such as Sonipat, Ghaziabad and Hisar. He was educated at Campus School in Hisar[12] and at Holy Child School at Sonipat.[13] In 1985, he took the IIT-JEE exam and secured All India Rank (AIR) of 563.[14] He graduated from Indian Institute of Technology Kharagpur, majoring in mechanical engineering.[15]
He joined Tata Steel in 1989 and was posted in Jamshedpur, Bihar (now in Jharkhand). Kejriwal resigned in 1992, having taken leave of absence to study for the Civil Services Examination.[12] He spent some time in Calcutta (present-day Kolkata), where he met Mother Teresa, and volunteered with The Missionaries of Charity and at the Ramakrishna Mission in North-East India and at Nehru Yuva Kendra.[16][17]
IRS[edit | edit source]
Arvind Kejriwal joined the Indian Revenue Service (IRS) as an Assistant Commissioner of Income Tax in 1995, after qualifying through the Civil Services Examination.[18][19][20] In February 2006, he resigned from his position as Joint Commissioner of Income Tax in New Delhi.[18]
In 2012, Arvind Kejriwal founded the Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) to fight corruption and improve governance. The party made its mark in the 2013 Legislative Assembly election, but his first government lasted only 49 days. In 2015, Kejriwal returned with a decisive victory, focusing on education, healthcare, and welfare. He was re-elected in 2020, further cementing his leadership in Delhi. However, his defeat in 2025 in Delhi polls revealed his short comings. Since 2012, he has acted as the main national convenor of AAP.
Activism[edit | edit source]
Parivartan and Kabir[edit | edit source]
In December 1999, while still in service with the Income Tax Department, Kejriwal, Manish Sisodia and others founded a movement named Parivartan (which means "change"), in the Sundar Nagar area of Delhi. A month later, in January 2000, Kejriwal took a sabbatical from work to focus on Parivartan.[21][22]
Parivartan addressed citizens' grievances related to Public Distribution System (PDS), public works, social welfare schemes, income tax and electricity. It was not a registered NGO - it ran on individual donations, and was characterised as a jan andolan ("people's movement") by its members.[23] Later, in 2005, Kejriwal and Manish Sisodia launched Kabir, a registered NGO named after the medieval philosopher Kabir. Like Parivartan, Kabir was also focused on RTI and participatory governance. However, unlike Parivartan, it accepted institutional donations. According to Kejriwal, Kabir was mainly run by Sisodia.[24]
In 2000, Parivartan filed a public interest litigation (PIL) demanding transparency in public dealings of the Income Tax department, and also organised a satyagraha outside the Chief Commissioner's office.[25] Kejriwal and other activists also stationed themselves outside the electricity department, asking visitors not to pay bribes and offered to help them in getting work done for free.[26]
In 2001, the Delhi government enacted a state-level Right To Information (RTI) Act, which allowed the citizens to access government records for a small fee. Parivartan used RTI to help people get their work done in government departments without paying a bribe. In 2002, the group obtained official reports on 68 public works projects in the area, and performed a community-led audit to expose misappropriations worth ₹ 7 million in 64 of the projects.[22] On 14 December 2002, Parivartan organised a Jan sunvai (public hearing), in which the citizens held public officials and leaders accountable for the lack of development in their locality.[27]
In 2003 (and again in 2008[28]), Parivartan exposed a PDS scam, in which ration shop dealers were siphoning off subsidised foodgrains in collusion with civic officials. In 2004, Parivartan used RTI applications to access communication between government agencies and the World Bank, regarding a project for privatisation of water supply. Kejriwal and other activists questioned the huge expenditure on the project and argued that it would hike water tariffs ten-fold, thus effectively cutting off the water supply to the city's poor. The project was stalled as a result of Parivartan's activism. Another campaign by Parivartan led to a court order that required private schools, which had received public land at discounted prices, to admit more than 700 poor kids without a fee.[25][26]
Along with other social activists like Anna Hazare, Aruna Roy and Shekhar Singh, Kejriwal came to be recognised as an important contributor to the campaign for a national-level Right to Information Act (enacted in 2005).[25] He resigned from his job in February 2006, and later that year, he was given the Ramon Magsaysay Award for Emergent Leadership, for his involvement with Parivartan.[29] The award recognised him for activating the RTI movement at the grassroots and empowering New Delhi's poor citizens to fight corruption.[26]
By 2012, Parivartan was largely inactive. Sundar Nagri, where the movement was concentrated, suffered from irregular water supply, unreliable PDS system and poorly done public works.[23] Calling it "ephemeral and delusionary in nature", Kejriwal noted that Parivartan's success was limited, and the changes brought by it did not last long.[30]
Public Cause Research Foundation[edit | edit source]
In December 2006, Kejriwal established the Public Cause Research Foundation in December 2006, together with Manish Sisodia and Abhinandan Sekhri. He donated his Ramon Magsaysay Award prize money as a seed fund. Besides the three founders, Prashant Bhushan and Kiran Bedi served as the Foundation's trustees.[31] This new body paid the employees of Parivartan.[23] Kejriwal used the RTI Act in corruption cases in many government departments including the Income Tax Department, the Municipal Corporation of Delhi, the Public Distribution System and the Delhi Electricity Board.[16]
Jan Lokpal movement[edit | edit source]
In 2010, Kejriwal protested against corruption in the Commonwealth Games. He argued that the Central Vigilance Commission (CVC) did not have any powers to take any action against the guilty, while CBI was incapable of launching an unbiased investigation against the ministers who controlled it. He advocated appointment of public ombudsman - Lokpal at the Centre and Lokayuktas in states.[32]
In 2011, Kejriwal joined several other activists, including Anna Hazare and Kiran Bedi, to form the India Against Corruption (IAC) group. The IAC demanded enactment of the Jan Lokpal Bill, which would result in a strong ombudsman. The campaign evolved into the 2011 Indian anti-corruption movement. In response to the campaign, the government's advisory body - the National Advisory Council - drafted a Lokpal Bill. However, the NAC's Bill was criticised by Kejriwal and other activists on the grounds that it did not have enough powers to take action against the prime minister, other corrupt officeholders, and the judiciary. The activists also criticised the procedure for the selection of Lokpal, the transparency clauses and the proposal to disallow the Lokpal from taking cognizance of public grievances.[33]
Amid continuing protests, the Government constituted a committee to Draft a Jan Lokpal Bill. Kejriwal was one of the civil society representative members of this committee. However, he alleged that the IAC activists had an unequal position in the committee, and the government appointees kept ignoring their recommendations. The Government argued that the activists could not be allowed to blackmail the elected representatives through protests. Kejriwal retorted that democratically elected representatives could not be allowed to function like dictators, and asked for a public debate on the contentious issues.[34]
The IAC activists intensified their protests, and Anna Hazare organised a hunger strike. Kejriwal and other activists were arrested for defying a police directive to give a written undertaking that they will not go to JP Park. Kejriwal attacked the government on this and said there was a need for a debate over police power to detain and release people at will.[35][36] In August 2011, a settlement was reached between the Government and the activists.[37]
Besides the government, the Jan Lokpal movement was also criticised by some citizens as 'undemocratic' on the grounds that the ombudsman had powers over elected representatives. Arundhati Roy claimed that the movement was not a people's movement; instead, it was funded by foreigners to influence policymaking in India. She pointed out that the Ford Foundation had funded the Emergent Leadership category of the Ramon Magsaysay Award, and also donated $397,000 to Kejriwal's NGO Kabir.[38] Both Kejriwal and Ford Foundation termed the allegations as baseless, stating that the donations were made to support the RTI campaigns. Besides, several other Indian organisations had also received grants from the Ford Foundation.[39][40] Kejriwal also denied the allegations that the movement was a plot against the ruling Congress by the RSS, or that it was an upper-caste conspiracy against the Dalits.[24]
By January 2012, the Government had backtracked on its promise to implement a strong Jan Lokpal, resulting in another series of protests from Kejriwal and his fellow activists. These protests attracted lower participation compared to the 2011 protests.[41] By mid-2012, Kejriwal had replaced Anna Hazare as the face of the remaining protestors.[42] In January 2014, Kejriwal said that he will quit from the government if Jan Lokpal Bill is not passed.[43] In 2015, during the second term of the AAP government in Delhi, the Jan Lokpal Bill was passed by the assembly awaiting the president's approval.[44]
National Convener of AAP[edit | edit source]
One of the major criticisms directed at the Jan Lokpal activists was that they had no right to dictate terms to the elected representatives. As a result, Kejriwal and other activists decided to enter politics and contest elections.[45] In November 2012, they formally launched the Aam Aadmi Party; Kejriwal was elected as the party's National Convener. The party name reflects the phrase Aam Aadmi, or "common man", whose interests Kejriwal proposed to represent.[46] The establishment of AAP caused a rift between Kejriwal and Hazare.[47]
AAP decided to contest the 2013 Delhi Legislative Assembly election, with Kejriwal contesting against the incumbent Chief Minister Sheila Dikshit. Kejriwal became the fifth most-mentioned Indian politician on social media channels in the run-up to the elections.[48]
Chief Minister of Delhi[edit | edit source]
First term[edit | edit source]
In the 2013, Delhi Legislative Assembly elections for all 70 seats, the Bharatiya Janata Party won 31 seats, followed by Aam Aadmi Party with 28 seats.[49] Kejriwal defeated incumbent Chief Minister, Sheila Dikshit of the Indian National Congress (INC), in her constituency of New Delhi[50] by a margin of 25,864 votes.[51]
AAP formed a minority government in the hung assembly, (claiming support for the action gauged from opinion polls) with outside support from the eight INC MLAs, one Janata Dal MLA and one independent MLA.[52][53] Kejriwal was sworn in as the second-youngest chief minister of Delhi on 28 December 2013, after Chaudhary Brahm Prakash who became chief minister at the age of 34.[54][55] He was in charge of Delhi's home, power, planning, finance, services and vigilance ministries.[56]
On 14 February 2014, he resigned as Chief Minister after failing to table the Jan Lokpal Bill in the Delhi Assembly. He recommended the dissolution of the Assembly.[57] Kejriwal blamed the Indian National Congress and the Bharatiya Janata Party for stalling the anti-corruption legislation and linked it with the government's decision to register a First Information Report (FIR) against industrialist Mukesh Ambani, chairman and managing director of Reliance Industries.[58] In April 2014 he said that he had made a mistake by resigning without publicly explaining the rationale behind his decision.[59]
Second term[edit | edit source]
Kejriwal led Aam Aadmi Party won 67 of the 70 constituencies in the 2015 Delhi Assembly elections, leaving the BJP with three seats and the INC with none.[60] In those elections, he was again elected from the New Delhi constituency, defeating Nupur Sharma by 31,583 votes.[61] He took oath on 14 February 2015 as Delhi's chief minister for a second time at Ramlila Maidan.[62][63] Since then his party has passed the Jan Lokpal Bill though with some differences.[44][64]
There has been a long-running dispute between Kejriwal's office and that of the Lieutenant-Governor of Delhi during Kejriwal's second term as Chief Minister. Various issues have been involved, relating which office has ultimate responsibility for various aspects of government, including some significant public appointments. Manish Sisodia characterised it as "a battle between the selected and the elected" and indicated after a legal setback that the government was prepared to take the issues to the Supreme Court of India.[65]
Mohalla Clinics that are primary health centres in Delhi was first set up by the Aam Aadmi Party government in 2015, and as of 2018, 187[66] such clinics have been set up across the state and served more than 2 million residents.[67] The Government has kept a target of setting up 1000 such clinics in the city before 2020 Delhi Legislative Assembly Elections. Mohalla Clinics offer a basic package of essential health services including medicines, diagnostics, and consultation free of cost.[68] These clinics serve as the first point of contact for the population, offer timely services, and reduce the load of referrals to secondary and tertiary health facilities in the state.[69] Beginning in October 2019, New Delhi began rolling out free bus transit for women on the Delhi Transport Corporation, with women travelling for free when using pink tickets carrying a message from Kejriwal.[70] He has been criticised for his controversial remarks over Biharis and "outsiders".[71][72][73]
Shunglu Committee submitted a report to LG of Delhi raising questions over decisions of Government of Delhi.[74]
Third term[edit | edit source]
AAP won 62 seats out of 70 in the 2020 Delhi Legislative Assembly election. He took oath on 16 February 2020 as Delhi's chief minister for a third time at Ramlila Maidan, equalling the record of Sheila Dikshit.[75] On 21 March 2024, he became the first ever sitting chief minister in India to be arrested and imprisoned.[3][76] After being released on bail by the Supreme Court, he vowed to resign from the post of chief minister on 15 September 2024 to campaign for the upcoming Delhi assembly elections.[9] He resigned formally on 17 September 2024[77] and AAP named education minister Atishi Marlena as his replacement.[78]
COVID-19 Mismanagement[edit | edit source]
During the COVID-19 pandemic in India in April 2021, Congress accused the Kejriwal government of spending significant amounts on publicity campaigns while failing to augment oxygen storage capacity and set up new oxygen plants in the National Capital Territory over the preceding year.[79] A Central government-appointed committee criticised the Aam Aadmi Party (AAP)-led Delhi government for using state funds for advertisements that promoted Chief Minister Arvind Kejriwal and his party, allegedly violating Supreme Court guidelines.[80]
In a reply to a Right to Information (RTI) query, it was revealed that funds were allocated in December 2020 to establish eight oxygen plants in Delhi, but only one plant was completed. The remaining funds were reportedly diverted to advertising expenditures. During the oxygen crisis in 2021, the central government increased oxygen allocations for Delhi, prompting Kejriwal to publicly thank the central government for providing 730 tons of oxygen.[81][82] Critics accused Kejriwal of being "criminally liable" for the deaths of several patients in two Delhi hospitals due to oxygen shortages.[83]
In July 2022, a Supreme Court-appointed audit panel concluded that the Delhi government had exaggerated its oxygen requirements by four times during the second wave of the COVID-19 pandemic.[84]
Attack by BJP members[edit | edit source]
On 30 March 2022, the official residence of Delhi Chief Minister Arvind Kejriwal was attacked by a group of BJP supporters during a protest. Deputy Chief Minister Manish Sisodia alleged that the incident was part of a conspiracy to murder Kejriwal.[85][86]
Following the incident, AAP MLA Saurabh Bhardwaj filed a petition in the Delhi High Court seeking the constitution of a Special Investigation Team (SIT) to investigate the attack. The petition claimed that the attack appeared to have been carried out with the "tacit complicity" of the Delhi Police.[87] It alleged that the attackers breached the security cordon, damaged property including CCTV cameras, and vandalised the residence while police personnel failed to intervene.[87]
On 31 March 2022, eight individuals involved in the attack were arrested. Charges under provisions related to obstructing public servants and damaging public property were filed. The Delhi High Court observed that the security arrangements at the Chief Minister's residence were inadequate to control the crowd and sought a status report from the Delhi Police on their investigation into the incident.[88][87]
2024 arrest[edit | edit source]
After skipping nine summons from the Enforcement Directorate (ED), Delhi Chief Minister Arvind Kejriwal was arrested on 21 March 2024 by the ED after the Delhi High Court rejected his anticipatory bail in connection with the Delhi liquor policy money laundering case.[89][90] This made him the first sitting chief minister of India to be arrested (all others arrested before him had resigned from their post before being arrested).[91][92] The opposition alliance called it a fabricated case and "match-fixing" before the 2024 general elections by the Bharatiya Janata Party led union government.[5] The Delhi High Court dismissed Kejriwal's petition against his arrest and all his bail requests. The Supreme Court ultimately granted him interim bail from 10 May 2024 to 1 June 2024 on account of campaigning for the elections.[7][93][94]
Following the end of his interim bail and failure to extend it on medical grounds, Kejriwal surrendered at Tihar Jail on 2 June.[94] He was then sent to judicial custody until 5 June 2024.[94][95] A Delhi court denied the plea filed by Kejriwal seeking a seven-day interim bail and extended judicial custody until 19 June and subsequently till 3 July 2024.[96][97] On 20 June 2024 Kejriwal was granted bail by the trial court on a bail bond of 100,000 INR. However, his bail was put on hold before his release as ED appealed against it in the Delhi Hight Court.[98] Kejriwal was then questioned for 3 days by the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) and arrested on 26 June 2024 from Tihar Jail in the same case. Subsequently, he was sent to judicial custody till 12 July.[99][100]
On 12 July 2024, the Supreme Court granted interim bail to Kejriwal in money laundering case related to the alleged excise policy scam. However, he remained in jail due to the CBI arrest made in the previous month.[101][102] On 5 September 2024, the Supreme court reserved an order on his bail in the CBI case.[103] The reserved order was pronounced by the SC on 13 September 2024, granting him bail and ultimately leading to his release from Tihar Jail after five months.[8] However he served in prison for more than 5 months.[104]

Views[edit | edit source]
Kejriwal discussed his views on corruption and the state of the Indian democracy in his book Swaraj. He advocates for a decentralisation of government and the involvement of the panchayat in local decisions and budgets. He claims that foreign multinational corporations have too much power in the decision-making process of the central government and that the politicians at the centre are not being held accountable for their actions and inaction after their election.[30]
Personal life[edit | edit source]
In 1995, Kejriwal married Sunita, a 1993-batch IRS officer. She took voluntary retirement in 2016 as Commissioner of Income Tax in the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal.[citation needed]
The couple have a daughter and a son. Kejriwal follows Hinduism.[105] Kejriwal is a vegetarian and has been practising the Vipassanā meditation technique for many years.[12] He is diabetic.[106] In 2016, he underwent a surgery for his persistent cough problem.[107]
Kejriwal considers himself an Ambedkarite and calls himself a 'devotee' of B. R. Ambedkar.[108][109]
Controversies[edit | edit source]
COVID-19[edit | edit source]
In May 2021, Kejriwal called for the Indian central government to immediately stop air travel between India and Singapore, and develop "vaccine alternatives for children", due to "a new variant of coronavirus found in Singapore" which "is being said to be very dangerous for children".[110][111][112] However, the Singapore Health Ministry stated that there was no known Singaporean variant of COVID-19; a recent report discussing the threat of COVID-19 to Singaporean children was discussing a variant of COVID-19 first detected in India: B.1.617.[110] Many of the recent COVID-19 cases in Singapore were of B.1.617. Further, it said “There is no truth whatsoever in the assertions found within the reports”.[113] The foreign minister of India, Subrahmanyam Jaishankar, and the foreign minister of Singapore, Vivian Balakrishnan, criticised Kejriwal's comment as "irresponsible" and counter-factual respectively.[114][115]
In 2022, the Kejriwal government was accused by a central government panel of inflating the reported oxygen need of Delhi during the second wave of COVID-19 infections.[116][117][118][119]
Lawsuits[edit | edit source]
Several defamation cases were filed against Arvind Kejriwal by his political opponents. In January 2014, Kejriwal released a list of most corrupt politicians that included several leaders across the political spectrum.[120] Of the several on the list, Nitin Gadkari immediately filed a defamation suit against Kejriwal. Subsequently, Kejriwal apologised to union minister Nitin Gadkari for his unverified allegations and also sought apology from former minister Kapil Sibal.[121][122][123]
In 2016, Kejriwal made allegations against Bikram Majithia, the then revenue minister of Punjab of involvement in drug trade for which Majithia filed a defamation case against him and two others from Aam Aadmi party.[124][125] Kejriwal apologised to Majithia a couple of years later in March 2018.[126][127][128]
Kejriwal made allegations against finance minister Arun Jaitley for irregularities in DDCA. Arun Jaitley filed a 10-crore defamation suit against Kejriwal. On 2 March 2016, Delhi High Court asked Chief Minister Arvind Kejriwal and suspended BJP MP Kirti Azad to file their written statements in a civil defamation suit of Rs 5 crores filed by DDCA for their alleged remarks against the cricket body regarding its functioning and finances.[129][130][131][132] Following this, in April 2018 Arvind Kejriwal and three others from his party including Sanjay Singh, Raghav Chaddha and Ashutosh apologised to Arun Jaitley in a joint letter.[133][134]
In his affidavit to Election Directorate before the second term elections in 2015 Kejriwal had declared that he has 10 criminal charges and 47 total charges against him.[135][136]
In 2021, a Delhi court dismissed an assault case filed by a Delhi bureaucrat against Kejriwal and ten AAP MLAs and discharged them of all charges. The court noted that "no prima facie case" was made against them.[137]
In February 2024, Kejriwal was involved in a defamation lawsuit and issued an apology to the Supreme Court of India for retweeting YouTuber Dhruv Rathee's 2018 video on BJP IT Cell. The Delhi high court, in its earlier ruling had stated that sharing "purportedly libelous" content would fall under defamation laws.[138][139] On 11 March 2025, a Delhi court ordered an FIR against Arvind Kejriwal for allegedly misusing public money on large hoardings[140]
Official residence renovations[edit | edit source]
In late April 2023, BJP made allegations that Kejriwal had misappropriated public funds for renovations of his residence in Delhi.[141][142] An investigation was announced on 29 April 2023.[143][144][145] CBI said that they started investigating money spent on renovating Chief Minister Arvind Kejriwal’s house complex. Its Vigilance Department said it was pursuing misappropriation of funds and financial irregularities.[146][147][148][149][150][151]
